name: cross-graph diamond runs its fan-in once: each sender wave is one cause and one receiver wave
topology: A and D in graph g1; B and C in graph g2. Wire edge group ga carries edge a (A) from g1 to g2, and B and C depend on its inbound a; group gbc carries edges b (B) and c (C) from g2 to g1, and D depends on its inbound b and c: a diamond split across two single-threaded graphs. The test carries each group's frames by hand.
input: Subscribe D, which opens both sessions, and deliver the first causes. Write A and deliver each frame. Write A twice more, holding gbc's frames back, then deliver the two together.
expect: The first causes carry the values at subscription, so D starts on B's and C's values over A. Each write of A is one g1 wave and one ga cause; its delivery is one g2 wave in which B and C each run once, and gbc sends one cause carrying both b and c. That cause's delivery is one g1 wave in which D runs once, on B's and C's values from the same A, and its sinks get one array; D never runs on one new and one old leg. The two held causes are delivered as two g1 waves, in order.
note: Rewritten on 2026-11-11 for R-bridge@1 (graphrefly:D803): a cause is a sender wave and travels as one frame, so the return legs no longer arrive as separate frames in either order. The D798 text and the earlier text and evidence are in git history. Reference-module tests in reference/modules/bridge.test.mjs are candidate evidence only, not runtime evidence.
harness: Pending per-runtime owner qualification; no runtime test is claimed for this text.

name: a wire edge group releases each cause whole, in order and at most once per session
topology: A sender graph with an outbound wire edge group over edges x and y (state nodes); a receiver graph with the inbound group for x and y, a fan-in F over inbound x and y, and the group's issues node. The test carries frames by hand and can hand the receiver frames it builds.
input: Open the session and deliver the first cause. Write x; write x, then y, in separate waves; write x and y in one batch; let x's node send two arrays in one wave; invalidate x and complete y. End the outbound node's lifetime and open a new one while x has no value; again after y has completed; again after x has lost its value and completed. Hand the receiver a duplicate of a released cause, an older cause, a cause two past the last, a frame with an undeclared edge, one with PENDING or RESOLVED in an array, one with an array after a terminal in the same frame, one with arrays for the ended y, and one bearing another group's name. After a cause that carried only x, subscribe a new sink to inbound y. Give the outbound group an edge value that is not bytes.
expect: The first cause carries x's and y's snapshots. Each sender wave in which an edge sent is one cause carrying only the edges that sent, with their arrays in order (two arrays stay two). Each delivery is one receiver wave: the carried edges send their arrays from their inbound nodes, the others send nothing, and F runs once; the INVALIDATE and the COMPLETE arrive as the inbound nodes' own. The new session starts the count at 1, and its first cause carries an INVALIDATE for x. After y completed, the new session's first cause repeats y's snapshot and COMPLETE: inbound y has ended, so they are skipped without an issue, and x's INVALIDATE is released. After x lost its value and completed, the first cause carries an INVALIDATE ahead of x's COMPLETE, so inbound x ends without the old value. The duplicate and the older cause are dropped; the cause two past the last is released and the gap reported; the bad frames are refused whole and their numbers taken; the arrays for the ended y, which do not end with a terminal, are skipped, the rest of their frame released and the divergence reported; the frame bearing another group's name is ignored by this group. Each drop, gap, refusal and divergence is a value of the issues node, and no inbound node ends or fails because of one. The new sink on inbound y gets y's last released value. The value that is not bytes is a throw, so an ERROR, of the outbound node. No timer is set, and nothing goes up either graph.
note: Rewritten on 2026-11-11 for R-bridge@1 (graphrefly:D803): one frame per cause replaces per-edge PENDING and DATA frames, so incomplete, competing and data-before-pending causes no longer exist, and causes numbered in a session replace bounded tombstones. The D501-D562 text and its runtime evidence are in git history. Reference-module tests in reference/modules/bridge.test.mjs are candidate evidence only, not runtime evidence. Revised on 2026-11-11 for R-bridge@2 (graphrefly:D804): an ended inbound edge's arrays are skipped instead of refusing the frame, and an edge without a value gets an INVALIDATE ahead of its terminal.
harness: Pending per-runtime owner qualification; no runtime test is claimed for this text.

name: INVALIDATE through a diamond: one INVALIDATE out, private state kept, policy decides who runs
topology: State S; B and C over S; D over [B, C] keeps a running count in private state. Two variants of D: the default auto INVALIDATE policy, and the manual policy.
input: Write S so D holds a value and a nonzero count. Invalidate S, then write S again.
expect: The INVALIDATE reaches D on both legs in one wave and D sends exactly one INVALIDATE with the PENDING prefix. Under auto D's function does not run for it, D loses its value and keeps its private state, so the next write continues the count. Under manual D's function runs once with both inputs marked invalidated and sends the one INVALIDATE itself, deciding what to clear. A node with no value drops an INVALIDATE; the write after it reaches D as ordinary input.

name: a sync leg and an async leg: the async result is a later wave, nothing waits across it
topology: State A; B over A answers synchronously; C over A starts asynchronous work and sends its result later through ctx.down; D over [B, C].
input: Write A; let C's work finish; then write A again and close C's lifetime before the second result arrives.
expect: In A's wave C sends nothing, so it settles with the kernel's RESOLVED; D runs once, seeing B's new value and C's old one, and no PENDING stays open while the work runs. C's result is a new wave from C, in which D runs once more. The result that arrives after C's lifetime closed is dropped. Waiting for both legs before running is sugar in each language package (a gate), not kernel behavior.

name: PAUSE lockset multi-source
topology: node N with two independent pause controllers, A and B.

name: INVALIDATE arriving at a paused compute node
topology: compute node N = ([D1,D2], fn) paused via its own lockset (default/'true' mode); D1, D2 are sources. fn guards SENTINEL deps (reads prevData/data, emits only when present).
input: Three runs. (a) SOLE-DEP CANCEL: N has run once; PAUSE N; D1 settles [[DATA,v1]] (buffered, N does not recompute); D1 sends [[INVALIDATE]]; RESUME N. (b) RE-ARM: PAUSE N; D1 [[DATA,v1]]; D1 [[INVALIDATE]]; D1 [[DATA,v2]]; RESUME N. (c) MULTI-DEP SURVIVE: PAUSE N; D1 [[DATA,v1]]; D2 [[DATA,v2]]; D1 [[INVALIDATE]]; RESUME N.
expect: (a) the INVALIDATE PROPAGATES downstream immediately while paused (N broadcasts INVALIDATE, cache→SENTINEL, onInvalidate fires); on RESUME N does NOT recompute (the paused dep-wave was superseded — N is SENTINEL, nothing to recompute) — NO spurious undirty RESOLVED, and crucially NO recompute against a SENTINEL dep (so a non-guarding fn does NOT panic→spurious terminal ERROR). (b) on RESUME N recomputes ONCE with D1=v2 (the post-INVALIDATE DATA re-armed the buffer; v1 was superseded). (c) on RESUME N recomputes ONCE with D2=v2 and D1=SENTINEL (the fn guards D1) — the D1 INVALIDATE did not cancel the recompute D2's buffered change warrants (no lost update). In all cases the downstream dirty bookkeeping stays balanced (N's leading DIRTY is cleared by either the INVALIDATE or the resume settle).

topology: Sources A and B feed N, which records what ctx.deps shows it.
input: (a) Write B only. (b) Make A send RESOLVED alone. (c) A sends [DATA 1, DATA 2, INVALIDATE, DATA 3] in one array. (d) A sends DATA null, then DATA []. (e) A completes; B ends with ERROR e. (f) A node sends DATA SENTINEL.
expect: For each dependency ctx.deps[i] gives its id, this run's arrays as DATA payloads in order (a RESOLVED array is []), its terminal in this run or null, and the latest value received. (a) A's entry has no arrays. (b) A's entry has one empty array. (c) The array is split at its last INVALIDATE: what came before is dropped, and N sees [3]. (d) null and [] are ordinary payloads. (e) The terminals are A's COMPLETE and B's ERROR e; they never appear among the arrays. (f) DATA SENTINEL is rejected. Under the manual INVALIDATE policy ctx.deps[i] also says whether an INVALIDATE arrived. Reading only some dependencies is sugar.

name: the message set is closed: PULL, PAUSE, RESUME and TEARDOWN are not messages
topology: State A; node N over A; a sink on N.
input: N's function sends [PULL], [PAUSE, L], [RESUME, L] and [TEARDOWN], each in a separate run; N sends a well-formed DATA after them.
expect: Each of the four is an unknown message type and is rejected, ending N with ERROR at the first of them; nothing of it reaches the sink. Control such as pausing, demand or restart is a write to a state node the target declares as a dependency, so it travels as ordinary DATA on a declared edge; nothing travels up the graph.

name: PULL invokes holder even without dep change and params may drive retained output
topology: A pullable retained-view holder SNAP holds pullId P and has stable retained state plus a cursor/page helper. A downstream consumer C depends on SNAP and issues routed ctx.up([[PULL,{pullId:P,params}]]) demands. A plain snapshot-helper variant over the same holder exists to show no-change silent as helper policy. All intra-graph (D22).
input: 1) SNAP has already settled retained state and is quiet. 2) C issues PULL(P,{limit:1}). 3) Without any intervening dep DIRTY/DATA/RESOLVED/INVALIDATE, C issues PULL(P,{limit:2}). 4) Repeat with the plain snapshot-helper variant. 5) Attempt RESUME(P) as a negative control.
expect: Both PULLs are accepted as tier-1 control/demand and invoke the holder when serviceable, with ctx.pull.params observed as {limit:1} and then {limit:2}. The retained-view helper may emit two ordinary downstream DIRTY-before-DATA DATA pages computed from the two params over unchanged retained state/cursor. The plain snapshot-helper variant may emit nothing on the second no-change demand, but this silence is helper policy after holder invocation, not substrate suppression of PULL. Params never travel as DATA-up or as an independent downstream message. RESUME(P) does not invoke the holder and does not install ctx.pull.
note: D278 / spec-amend. This scenario pins the distinction needed by messaging catalog/deadLetter snapshots and subscription.available: PULL is a holder-invocation demand with optional params; downstream DATA is an ordinary holder/helper output decision. It prevents the old C-16 no-change-silent facet from becoming a substrate rule that would make parameterized retained views impossible. | Rust ARM GREEN 2026-06-15: graphrefly-rs crates/graphrefly/tests/conformance.rs::c27_pull_invokes_holder_without_dep_change_and_params_drive_output covers repeated no-change PULL invocation with params-driven retained output and RESUME negative control. | TS ARM GREEN 2026-06-16: packages/ts/src/__tests__/conformance.test.ts C-27 covers repeated no-change PULL holder invocation, params-driven retained output, plain-helper silence as helper policy, and RESUME negative control. | Python ARM GREEN 2026-06-22 after D454: graphrefly-py tests/test_conformance.py::test_c27_pull_family_public_no_change_params_drive_output_and_plain_silence covers repeated no-change public PULL holder invocation, ctx.pull_params-driven retained output over stable state, plain snapshot-helper silence as helper policy after holder invocation, and RESUME negative control.

name: Intact output arrays, kernel-only PENDING prefixes and written order
topology: Diamond A->B,C->D with two sinks on A.
input: A's function sends DATA23, DATA23, DATA30 in one ctx.down; compare three separate ctx.down calls and a host batch of three sets. One sink callback requests a set and a subscription. A node function sends an array containing PENDING, and another sends [DATA 1, INVALIDATE, DATA 2, DATA 3]. One function sends [DATA 2, RESOLVED] and another [RESOLVED] alone. In a host batch, stage DATA for a node, then submit RESOLVED and, after a COMPLETE, a DATA for it, catching both rejections. Open a batch from a sink callback. A sink throws after a commit.
expect: All three occurrences reach each sink in one array with one PENDING prefix, and D runs once after B and C settle, seeing them. Separate calls stay separate arrays, each with its own PENDING prefix; the batch delivers one accumulated array per node at commit. Sink requests run only after the whole fanout of the current wave, so no sink is cut off mid-array. ctx.down rejects output containing PENDING; uncaught, that is the node's ERROR. [DATA 1, INVALIDATE, DATA 2, DATA 3] is published as [PENDING, INVALIDATE] then [PENDING, DATA 2, DATA 3]. RESOLVED in node output is rejected, as PENDING is, and ends its node with ERROR: only the kernel sends RESOLVED, to a pending node that sent nothing. The caught rejections leave earlier staging unchanged, and the batch commits [PENDING, DATA, COMPLETE]. The batch opened from a callback stages its writes and commits after the current wave as one wave. The sink failure goes to the host reporter and rolls nothing back.

name: A batch delivers nothing before commit, and its topology requests follow the commit
topology: A->B with sink s on B; a second node C with a sink.
input: In one batch body: set A, subscribe a new sink t to B, rewire B to [A, C] through its ctx, and read A. Repeat with a body that sets A and then throws. Pass an async function as the body. Pass a plain function that sets A, awaits, and sets A again. In another body, open a nested batch that sets B and returns a value. In one batch body, set A with a function of its value, set A to a value, set A with a function again, invalidate A and set A with a function once more; in another, set B and set A with a function that throws. Set A with a function that returns the value it was given, and set A to its own value. From s's callback during a wave, the first time it runs, call batch with a body that reads A, sets A and returns a value.
expect: Nothing is delivered and nothing changes while the body runs; the read inside the body returns the retained value. When the body returns, the sets commit as one wave with PENDING prefixes; then the subscribe and the rewire run in request order, against the committed topology, before any request the commit wave itself makes, so t starts from the committed value. The throwing body delivers nothing and drops its sets and requests; there is no compensating RESOLVED. The nested batch joins the outer one: its set commits in the outer body's one commit wave, and it returns its body's value. The async function body is refused before any of it runs. The promise-returning body commits its synchronous set; the host reporter is told, and the set after the await is a later separate wave. Each function runs at the commit, in staging order: the first sees A's retained value, the second the value set before it, the third no value; the batch whose function throws commits nothing, not even its set of B. A function that returns the value it was given writes nothing and starts no wave; a plain value equal to A's is written and starts a wave. Called during a wave, the body runs at once and batch returns its value to the callback; its read sees the value retained so far, and its set commits as a later wave, after the current wave has reached every subscriber.

name: A pausable holds arrays until the last lock is released, and passes INVALIDATE and terminals at once
topology: State a, computed x over a, pausable p after x with a sink; a self-stopping source src that declares its lock state as a dependency.
input: Pause p; set a to 2 and then 3; resume. Pause p twice from the sink callback during the resume wave, then set a to 4; resume one of the two locks; resume a lock nobody holds. Write the lock state to hold a lock no handle has taken, as a restore brings it back, and resume that lock through the handle. Separately invalidate a while p is paused and then set a. Pause src before its first activation, subscribe to it, then resume; and let work that src started before a pause finish while paused. Separately, with p unpaused and then paused, write a and complete it in one batch, and write a and error it in one batch.
expect: While paused x keeps computing and p sends nothing; on resume p sends the two held arrays [PENDING, DATA 20] and [PENDING, DATA 30] in one wave, each as it arrived, without rerunning x. Both re-pauses are sets of the lock state with a function that apply after the resume wave, both locks are held, and the DATA from a = 4 stays held after one of them is resumed. Resuming a lock nobody holds writes nothing and starts no wave. The handle releases the lock that was only in the lock state: the lock state is the only copy. The INVALIDATE passes at once and discards what was held before it; x, built with the manual INVALIDATE policy, sees it once and the resume does not hand it to x again. src's function runs at activation to read the lock and starts no work; its sink gets [START], and after the resume src's work starts. Work started before the pause may still publish while paused. Unpaused, p forwards [PENDING, DATA, COMPLETE] and [PENDING, DATA, ERROR] unchanged; paused, only the terminal goes out, and what was held is discarded.

name: State keeps its value across close, a terminal seals it, and pause locks outlive the pausable
topology: State s with a sink; pausable p after s with a sink o; a source src with pausable q after it.
input: Set s, unsubscribe its last sink and queue a write behind the close; complete s and queue a write behind the terminal. Pause p, set s to 30, unsubscribe o, subscribe o again, resume. Pause q, let src send [DATA 30, COMPLETE] in one array, resume.
expect: The state keeps its value across close, and the write queued behind the close still applies. After COMPLETE the state is sealed: the queued write is dropped before it changes anything and reported to the host reporter, and a new subscriber receives [START, DATA, COMPLETE] with the sealed value. p's lock stays in its lock state after o leaves, so o's new subscription receives [START] only, and the resume sends [PENDING, DATA 30]. q passes the COMPLETE at once and discards the DATA 30 held with it; the resume sends nothing, and q's retained value stays the one it had before the pause.

name: A holder serves each pull once with the latest params and stays quiet between pulls
topology: State a, holder h after a with a sink and a service function; a pausable before a second holder.
input: Set a twice between pulls; pull with params p1; pull with nothing new; pull twice in one batch (p2 then p3); pull inside a batch whose body then throws; pull while h is inactive and then activate it; invalidate a while h holds values; resume the pausable before the second holder without a pull. In another graph write the demand state with a request numbered 5, as a restore brings it back, activate h and pull.
expect: Between pulls h's sink receives nothing, not even PENDING. The pull runs the service once with every array held since the last INVALIDATE and params p1; what it sends is a later wave. A pull with nothing new still runs the service, and if it sends nothing nothing goes out. The two pulls in one batch are served once, after the commit, with p3; the throwing batch serves nothing. The pull at the inactive holder neither activates it nor is kept, so activation serves nothing. The INVALIDATE discards what was held and reaches the sink as the holder's output, a later wave. A resume without a pull neither runs the second holder nor flushes what it holds. A later subscriber receives the last served value in its START. The request already in the demand state counts as served at activation; the pull after it is numbered 6, from the state's value, and is served.

name: A closed lifetime revokes old ctx, and cleanup failures stay isolated
topology: N depends on P, which depends on A, with a sink on N. P and N each have a setup that returns a cleanup; N's cleanup throws and reads N's private state. N's function keeps its ctx, records the value it ran on in private state, and starts work that calls ctx.down later.
input: Read N's status before it is subscribed, then subscribe a sink. Set A so that N runs a second time, invalidate A, and set it again. Unsubscribe the last sink while N's late work is pending; let the late work call the old ctx.down; subscribe again, read N's status from its cleanup during the deactivation and after the resubscription, and complete A. Separately, request the unsubscribe from inside N's function, and stage output in a batch through a lifetime that closes before the batch commits. Keep ctx and a dependency view after setup/function return; read each, including from a later invocation. In a batch stage a throwing updater, a late ctx.down and quiet synchronous output; separately throw from the body and close a lifetime before queued output runs.
expect: N's setup runs once per lifetime, before its first run; the second run runs no setup and drops no cleanup, and N's cleanup runs once at deactivation and reads the value of the last run. N's status is derived, not stored: inactive with an empty cache before the subscription, active and ready with a value, empty after the INVALIDATE, closing while its cleanup runs, and completed once A's COMPLETE has ended it. Deactivation releases N's dependencies first, so P's cleanup runs, then runs N's cleanup: its throw goes to the host reporter and the close completes. The old signal is aborted and private state is dropped. The old ctx.down is dropped. The new lifetime has a distinct ctx and signal, runs N's setup again and runs its function on fresh snapshots. An unsubscribe requested during an invocation waits until the wave ends. Output staged by a lifetime that closed before commit is dropped at commit, not retained. Expired dependency reads fail with "ctx.deps is only available during setup or function invocation" (or are statically unavailable); later invocations do not revive old views. Already captured data is usable. A failed commit drops host writes and quiet synchronous output but runs body late-output requests in order; a throwing body drops all its requests. Closed-lifetime output is dropped at execution. An ended host target refuses a queued batch before any updater, without partial writes.

name: Terminal fanout, the ended node's lifetime closing, and acquisition of an ended node
topology: Computed S over a state T that has no other dependent; S's setup returns a cleanup; sinks X and Y on S.
input: Set T so that S sends [DATA 1, COMPLETE] in one array; during the fanout X's callback subscribes Z to S and then throws.
expect: X and Y each receive the whole [PENDING, DATA 1, COMPLETE] array. After the fanout S's lifetime closes: it releases T, which deactivates, and its cleanup runs, while X and Y stay subscribed and S keeps its value and COMPLETE. Z's subscription runs after the fanout and receives [START, DATA 1, COMPLETE], the ended node's snapshot; S never runs again. X's throw goes to the host reporter and is not S's ERROR. Starting S again is not a kernel behavior: it is an inner node that a restart owner replaces.

name: Rewire keeps the instance and runs between waves
topology: D depends on B (cached) with a sink, and rewires itself through its ctx; its function reads its dependencies by id. C has a value; E has ended with COMPLETE.
input: Rewire D to [B, C]; then to [C, B]; then to [C]; then to [C] again; then add E. Rewire D to add G, a state with no value yet, then set G. Rewire D to no dependencies, then set B. From inside D's function, request a rewire. Rewire D to include itself, a duplicate, or a node that depends on D. Unsubscribe D's sink and subscribe again; rewire D through the ctx of the closed lifetime; let D end, then rewire it through its last ctx. In one batch body, replace X onto [Y] and Y onto [X], two nodes that each depend only on B; and from one sink callback, ask X's and Y's ctx to rewire each onto the other. Read dependency ids through ctx during the invocation and look them up in the owning graph.
expect: Adding C keeps D's values, private state, function, lifetime and sinks and sends no START; C's snapshot is one ordinary input wave, D's function runs once and C then drives D. Reordering keeps B's and C's records. Removing B releases it without a wave; it no longer drives D and D keeps its value. Rewiring to the current list does nothing. Adding the ended E delivers its snapshot, so its COMPLETE counts toward D's policy. Adding G, which has no snapshot, runs no function and D keeps its value; G's first value then drives D. Rewiring to no dependencies releases them without a wave, keeps D's value, and later writes to B no longer reach D. The rewire requested from D's function waits until the wave ends. Rewires to a self-dependency, a duplicate or a dependency that depends on D are refused. Throughout, D's declared dependencies (its definition) stay [B]; after the resubscription D is back on [B], the rewire through the closed lifetime's ctx is dropped, and so is the rewire after D ended, whose dependencies are back to [B]. Of the two replaces, and of the two rewires, the one that runs second would close a cycle that neither request alone makes: it is refused when it runs, its node keeps its dependencies, and the refusal goes to the host reporter as a queued request's failure. Each id is the graph-registered id used by find, describe and definition, not a separate arena-only identity.

name: A closed lifetime revokes old work while the node and topology remain

input: Rewire N to [A, B] through its ctx; let the late work call ctx.down. Start new late work, then unsubscribe and resubscribe N with the same dependencies, and let the old work call its ctx.down.

name: Restore keeps the saved state, refreshes once on a changed input, and reopens what a setup opened
topology: State a; computed p over a built from a recipe, with private state; a node built without a recipe; an ended node with dependencies; a recipe node that rewires itself for its lifetime; a timer source built from a recipe whose setup starts a timer and returns a cleanup that stops it, counting in private state.
input: Capture at a wave boundary and restore into a new graph; subscribe to p. Restore again, change a before the first subscription, then subscribe. Restore again, invalidate a and then set it before the first subscription; restore once more and complete a before the first subscription. Capture inside a wave and inside a batch body; capture a value, a private state or an ERROR payload that is not JSON; restore with a missing recipe; restore the node built without a recipe; restore a checkpoint without the record of what each node received, as one written to an earlier format. Replace a recipe node keeping its dependencies but changing its function; replace one with a recipe and another setup; replace one onto a dependency made after it; replace one without a recipe; let the rewiring node rewire itself; capture and restore after each. Restore the timer source, subscribe and let the timer fire. Capture a restored graph again before anything subscribes, and restore that. Remove the entire lifetime/received record from an open computed node with saved values. Capture a local-only active computed node holding a non-JSON value, private state or ERROR.
expect: Restore runs no function, sends nothing and gives the same topology description. The first subscription to p receives p's saved last-array values, and p has its saved private state, without p's function running. After a changed a, p's function runs once with only a as input; a run that sends nothing keeps the saved value. The INVALIDATE followed by a set before the first subscription is seen as the set alone. A dependency that only completed before the first subscription brings its COMPLETE without its values again. The ended node comes back ended with its dependencies and without private state, and a subscriber receives its terminal snapshot. Captures inside a wave or a batch body are refused, as are values, private state and payloads that are not JSON; a missing recipe, the local-only node and the checkpoint without received records fail the restore. A node replaced without a recipe is local-only, so it is not restored as its old recipe; one replaced with a recipe is restored as that recipe, with that instance's setup; one replaced onto a dependency made after it is restored after that dependency; the rewired node is restored onto its lifetime's dependencies. At its first activation the timer source's setup runs, starting one timer, and its function does not run; it counts on from its saved private state. The graph captured again before anything subscribed restores to the same state. No checkpoint carries revision or version evidence. The missing received record is refused even when its whole enclosing record is absent. Non-JSON capture is refused before local-only restore classification; a JSON local-only capture still fails at restore. Restoring never recreates retain subscriptions; the host explicitly retains before commands.

name: Revision evidence counts committed output, survives restore unchanged, and never wraps
topology: State a and an evens filter e over a, both observed by a revision observer with a hash; a restorable state and recipe node for the checkpoint variant.
input: Subscribe a second observer. Set a to an equal value, then to an odd value, invalidate a twice, complete a; error another state. Write two values in one batch. Capture the observer's positions beside a checkpoint, restore both, start a new observer from the saved positions and set a. Start an observer one below the limit and send an array of two values. Start one from an invalid saved position.
expect: Subscribing advances nothing. The equal DATA advances revision and valueRevision of a and e. The odd value advances a; e is settled by the kernel's RESOLVED, which advances only e's revision. The first INVALIDATE advances both positions of a and e; the second removes nothing, is not sent and advances nothing. COMPLETE and ERROR advance revision only. The batch of two values advances both positions by two. The hash agrees with the retained values after each step and describes absence after the INVALIDATE. After restore the positions are unchanged, and the next set advances them by one. The array that would pass the limit is refused whole, the positions stay, and the host reporter is told. The invalid saved position is refused.

name: An ended node can be subscribed and depended on
topology: S has sent DATA 1 and COMPLETE; T has sent ERROR e; both have no sinks.
input: Subscribe a sink to S. Create D over S with auto COMPLETE, and E over T with auto ERROR, and subscribe them. Create M over T with manual ERROR and manual COMPLETE. Set S. Replace D after it has ended.
expect: The sink receives [START, DATA 1, COMPLETE]. D's function runs once on S's snapshot and D completes after that run. E ends with ERROR e without running its function. M's function runs with T's ERROR as input and M stays open. S never changes again; the set on S is refused. The replace gives D a new instance: D's sink receives START and the new instance's snapshot after D's COMPLETE, since a terminal ends an instance, not the node. (A rewire through an ended node's ctx is dropped; see C-35.)

name: The snapshot is the node's last array that carried DATA
topology: Computed node N over A with a sink; state Q.
input: N sends [DATA 1], then [DATA 2, DATA 3], then a RESOLVED array; subscribe a late sink. Create a dependent of N. N sends [INVALIDATE] and another sink subscribes. Write Q twice in one batch; deactivate N and Q and reactivate them.
expect: The late sink receives [START, DATA 2, DATA 3]; the RESOLVED array does not replace the retained values. The dependent's first run sees N's waves [[2, 3]]. After the INVALIDATE a new sink receives [START] only. The batch is one array, so Q's snapshot carries both values. On reactivation N has no retained values until it runs again; Q keeps its values.

name: The message set is closed and nothing travels upstream
topology: A node N over A with a sink.
input: N's function calls ctx.down with arrays whose type is PAUSE, RESUME, PULL, TEARDOWN, PENDING, START or an unknown type, catching each rejection, and then sends DATA. Repeat one of them without catching.
expect: Each of those arrays is rejected by ctx.down before anything is applied, START because only the kernel sends it, at subscribe and at a replace; N's retained value is the DATA sent afterwards. Uncaught, the rejection is N's ERROR. There is no upward call on ctx. Pausing, demand and restart are built as nodes whose controller writes a state the target declares as a dependency.

name: A restart owner keeps one face downstream, serves each request once and makes no stale or hopeless attempt
topology: State a; a computed node u over a whose setup opens a resource; a restart owner r with its inner at r/inner over u, a sink s on r and a sink t on r/inner; rounds 2 and a retry policy of two attempts per round with a delay.
input: Let the inner complete twice, counting u's openings and closings. In a second graph let it fail once, then complete, then fail twice. Describe the topology before and after an attempt. Request a restart while the inner is live; unsubscribe s and subscribe it again; unsubscribe, request a restart while r is inactive, subscribe again, and request once more. Let the inner fail and, while its retry waits, request a restart; let the delay pass. Let the inner fail and unsubscribe s before the delay passes, then subscribe again. Let the inner fail and complete a while its retry waits. In another graph complete a while the inner is live. In another, write the restart state with 1, as a restore brings it back, subscribe s and request a restart.
expect: s receives the inner's values from both rounds and one COMPLETE, after the second completion only; u opens once and closes once, when r ends, since r holds it ahead of the inner; no terminal reaches s while a restart is possible. The first ERROR is retried after the delay, the count starts again in the next round, and the second ERROR of that round ends r with that ERROR. The topology description is unchanged across attempts and t receives START at each attempt. The request on a live inner starts a fresh one without releasing a; the resubscription starts exactly one fresh inner, the old request being served already; the request made while r was inactive starts nothing beyond the fresh inner of the next activation, and the request after it starts one attempt. A retry pending when the request started another attempt is dropped and does not replace it; a retry pending when r's lifetime closed is dropped, and the new activation starts a fresh inner. When a completes while a retry waits, no inner is started over it and r ends with the inner's ERROR; when a completes while the inner is live, r ends with the inner's COMPLETE. The restored request counts as served at activation; the request after it writes 2, from the state's value, and starts a fresh inner. A retry's timer is cleared when r's lifetime closes.

name: The kernel adds only the settling RESOLVED, a quiet node never holds a wave, and a wave of terminals holds a fan-in
topology: State A; F over A, which sends DATA only for an even value; a quiet node Q over A, which keeps its ctx; D over [A, Q]; sinks on F, Q and D.
input: Set A to 3. Set A to 2, where Q's function sends DATA during its run. Then call Q's kept ctx.down after the wave. Set A to 5, where Q sends nothing. Invalidate A. In a second graph, give D over two dependencies B and C of one state S a manual COMPLETE policy and complete S; in a third, give D the manual INVALIDATE policy instead and invalidate S.
expect: For 3, F was marked pending and sent nothing, so its sink receives one RESOLVED after PENDING, the only output the kernel adds; D runs once. For 2, Q is never marked pending: D runs once in A's wave without waiting for Q, and Q's output during its run goes out after that wave as a new wave of its own, which runs D again. The later ctx.down is a new wave too. For 5, Q sends nothing and no RESOLVED is added for it. The INVALIDATE reaches Q's sink and D's at once, in A's wave, each as [PENDING, INVALIDATE]. A terminal marks the cone pending like a value: D waits for both B's and C's COMPLETE, each arriving as [PENDING, COMPLETE], and its function runs once and sees both. In a third graph, give D the manual INVALIDATE policy and invalidate S: D waits for both legs and its function runs once, seeing both inputs invalidated.

name: History survives a checkpoint round trip
topology: State a and a history node h over a built from its recipe, subscribed and fed a few values.
input: Capture and restore; send more values to a. Restore again, subscribe, then invalidate a and send a value. Restore once more and complete a before the first subscription.
expect: The history node comes back with its saved list and goes on from it. It does not run at its first activation; under the manual INVALIDATE policy the INVALIDATE after that is its function's input and clears the list as in the original. A source that only completed before the first subscription brings its COMPLETE without its values again, so the list is not appended to. On each step the original and the restored graph send the same arrays.

name: Pause, demand and restart nodes survive a checkpoint round trip
topology: Built with recipes: a paused pausable holding arrays; a demand holder holding arrays after a served pull; a restart owner after an outside request; a restart owner waiting for a delayed retry.
input: Capture, restore, and give both graphs the same steps. Before the first subscription to the restored graph, make a pull at the restored holder and a restart request at the restored owner.
expect: No node of these graphs is local-only. The restored pausable holds the same locks and arrays and its resume sends them as the original's does. The restored holder serves the next pull with the held arrays and the next request number; a pull made while it was inactive is not served at its activation. The restored owner keeps its round, failures and request number, and a restart requested while it was inactive starts no attempt; the owner that was waiting for a retry renews its inner at its first activation instead of staying stuck, and the renewed inner runs. On each step both graphs send the same arrays.
note: Moved out of C-38 on 2026-11-10 (D802). Each clause waits for its module's own activation (R-pause, R-demand, R-restart); until then it checks draft rules. Reference-module tests are candidate evidence only.

name: graphs on one thread share no wave, request queue or batch
topology: Graphs g1 and g2 on one thread. In g1, state a with sink s1, and state c with a sink; in g2, state b with sink s2.
input: Write a. During a's wave, s1 writes b and, after that write returns, captures checkpoints of g1 and of g2. During b's wave, s2 writes c. Then, in one g1 batch body, write a, then b, and read b before the body returns.
expect: The write of b is not held by g1's wave: b's wave runs at once, inside s1's callback, and s2 sees b's new value before a's wave ends. The capture of g1, which is in its wave, is refused; the capture of g2, which is idle, succeeds. The write of c waits for g1's wave to end and then runs as g1's next request. In the batch, the write of b is g2's own request: it runs at once and the read sees b's new value; only the write of a commits, when the body returns.
note: Added on 2026-11-11 for R-graph-domain@3 (graphrefly:D803). The reference kernel and graphrefly-py keep this state per graph; TS and Rust shared it across the graphs of one thread (graphrefly-rs:D8). The reference tests named C-47 in reference/kernel/kernel.test.mjs and reference/modules/checkpoint.test.mjs are candidate evidence only.

name: the graph layer: find, describe, observe and retain
topology: State a; computed b over a (ten times a), c over a, and d over a, whose function keeps its ctx; nothing subscribed.
input: find b and an id that does not exist; describe the graph; observe [b] and set a; observe [b] a second time, stop the first observer and set a again; stop the second. Retain c twice and release each retain. Retain d, rewire d to [a, c] through its kept ctx, and describe again and read d's definition. Have a node deliver two arrays in one invocation and stop its observer from the first callback.
expect: find gives b and nothing for the unknown id. describe gives a, b, c, d in creation order, each exactly { id, kind, deps, quiet } (kind state for a, node for the others), and neither find nor describe activates b. The first observer activates b and receives one event per array, { id: b, msgs }: the START array with b's value first, then [PENDING, DATA 20]; there is no tier and no sequence number. After it stops it receives nothing more while the second goes on; after both stop, b is inactive. The first retain activates c, which stays active after the first release and deactivates after the second. After d's rewire, describe gives d's deps as [a, c], while d's definition still gives [a]. The observer receives no second array after stop; ordinary subscribe stop and retain release still take effect at wave end.
note: Added on 2026-11-11 for R-graph-surface@1 (graphrefly:D805). The reference test is in reference/modules/observe.test.mjs and is candidate evidence only. 2026-11-12: D808 adds rereview combination boundaries; runtime flags remain evidence claims pending owner qualification.
